Twelve years ago, the week before I left Australia, I couldn't sleep. So I [made a little D3 map](../2014-08-01-a-chapter-closes-a-chapter-opens/) of every flight I'd taken during my astrophysics postdoc — Dallas to Los Angeles to Melbourne, and everywhere that came after. It was a fun, late-night thing. I posted it and got on with the next chapter.

That map is gone now. It lived on bl.ocks.org, a little service for sharing D3 sketches, and when bl.ocks shut down it took the visualization with it. The old post still exists, but where the map used to be there's a dead embed.

::: {.column-margin}
bl.ocks.org rendered visualizations straight from GitHub gists. The service went away; the gist survived — which is the only reason I could rebuild this at all.
:::

I finally got around to fixing it. And since I was starting from scratch anyway, I pulled in the whole logbook — not just the postdoc, but every flight I have a record of, back to 2005.

::: {.column-page}
![Every flight I have a record of, 2005–2026. The map is Pacific-centered; arc opacity stacks, so the routes I've flown most often glow brightest.](/assets/images/flights/flights-map.svg)
:::

There's most of my adult life in that tangle. The bright knot on the right is home base drifting around the United States — Dallas, where I grew up; San Diego for grad school; and the dense little triangle of the Bay Area commute I could now draw from memory. The long arcs sweeping down across the Pacific are the Australia years. The threads reaching to Chile and Hawaii are observing runs — nights at the VLT in the Atacama and Keck on Mauna Kea, which at the time felt like the most exotic commute imaginable.

::: {.column-margin}
The faint lines to Santiago and Antofagasta are the road to Paranal; the ones to Honolulu and Kona are Keck.
:::

Seeing it all at once does something the individual trips never did. Each flight was just a flight — a red-eye, a layover, a bad sandwich. Drawn together they make a shape, and the shape is recognizably a life: where I came from, what I was chasing, who I was flying to see.

## How it's made (this time)

A note for anyone tempted to build one of these.

The 2014 version died for a reason worth remembering: it leaned on someone else's server and on JavaScript running live in your browser. When either one goes away, so does your map. This time I made the opposite bet. What you're looking at is a single static SVG — no scripts, no embeds, nothing phoning home. It's generated from my flight log by a [small Python program](https://github.com/jbwhit/website/tree/main/scripts/flights) and then it just... sits there. As long as the page renders, the map renders.

The other thing I was careful about: a flight log is more sensitive than it looks. Mine has booking references and seat numbers in it, and this site is public. So the only data that ships is the part that draws the picture — the airports, and how many times I've flown each route. No dates, no booking details, nothing that says where I'll be next Tuesday. The full log never leaves my laptop.

Ok future — twelve more years, and let's see what the map looks like then.
